study.title: Ezekiel 29 The judgment on Egypt and the care of God with Israel
study.overview: Ezekiel 29 brings together two messages against Egypt. In the first, God confronts Pharaoh for his arrogance and for the false confidence that Egypt inspired in Israel. Egypt is portrayed as a powerful force, but will be humiliated, emptied and scattered. In the second message, God recognizes Nebuchadnezzar's effort against Tyre and promises to give him Egypt as payment. The chapter ends with a pastoral promise: by reversing the humiliation of Egypt, God will also strengthen Israel and make Ezekiel speak more freely among the people, so that all may recognize the Lord.

outline.title: God opposes the pride of Pharaoh and the false security of Egypt
outline.explanation: The word begins with a date and the command to prophesy against Pharaoh and all Egypt. Pharaoh is described as a great monster from the rivers, saying that the Nile belongs to him and that he himself did. God responds with an image of capture, abandonment and death: the sovereign who judged himself lord of the waters will be plucked out of his dominion, exposed as prey and left as food. The spiritual motive is clear: Egypt was a fragile support for Israel, breaking who leaned against it, rather than sustaining it.

outline.title: The land of Egypt will be devastated, scattered, and then demolished
outline.explanation: God proclaims sword, destruction of men and beasts, desolation of the earth and forty years of dispersion among the nations. The arrogance of Egypt, expressed in the phrase that the river belongs to it, is the center of the accusation. After this period, Egypt will be gathered and restored to its land, but will not recover greatness: it will become a lower kingdom, incapable of dominating the nations. Thus it will cease to be a deceptive trust for Israel, and both will recognize that the Lord is God.

outline.title: Nebuchadnezzar receives Egypt as a reward for his service
outline.explanation: A new date introduces another prophetic word. The text recalls the long and exhausting campaign of Nebuchadnezzar against Tyre, which brought him tiredness, but no gain. Therefore God gives Egypt to the king of Babylon as compensation: he will plunder the land, take his wealth, and obtain the profit that he lacked in the previous campaign. The Babylonian empire, however, does not appear as the autonomous owner of history; the Lord himself states that he gave Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment for the work executed under his direction.

outline.title: The strengthening of Israel and the reopening of the prophet's mouth
outline.explanation: The chapter ends with a promise of restoration linked to the destiny of the nations. When the judgment on Egypt is fulfilled, the strength of the house of Israel will grow. The opening of Ezekiel's mouth in their midst indicates that his message will be confirmed and respected, and that the people will recognize again that the LORD is the one who governs history.

study.context: The notes place these messages on different dates from the exile of Jehoiakim/Jeconias: the first in the tenth year of captivity and the last in the twenty-seventh year. The commentators note that Ezekiel treats Egypt as a former enemy and also as an unstable ally of Judah, whose deceitful trust helped Israel to sin. The second oracle relates to Nebuchadnezzar's long campaign against Tyre and the subsequent weakening of Egypt, although the exact identification of some historical details and proper names depends on the commentators' reading.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes God's sovereignty over kings, empires, rivers, and historical periods. Egypt, which exalts itself as the origin of its own force, is shown as a creature before the Creator. Judgment is not only political, but moral and spiritual: pride and false trust receive divine response. At the same time, the Lord disciplines the nations for a purpose in relation to their people, undoing deceitful covenants and restoring Israel so that their name may be recognized. The expression of the Force of the house of Israel can be understood, in evangelical reading, as a sign of renewal given by God; the commentators link it to the image of a horn that springs, that is, growth of vigor, dignity and hope. The text also shows that God uses even a foreign king in his purposes, without ceasing to be the true Lord of history.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter shows that God has a main interest in his people: the fall of Egypt accompanies the revitalization of Israel, and the image of "make sprout a horn" points to renewal of strength and dignity.
Egypt had been to Israel a brittle support; therefore, the prophecy serves to ward off the people from trust in human covenants and show that the humiliation of Egypt lowers this false security.
The promise to restore Egypt as the lower "or inferior" implies, in the reading of the commentator, that he will remain in a tax and subordinate position, without regaining ancient supremacy.

questions: In which areas do I still treat human alliances, resources or influences as my primary security, rather than trusting the Lord?
What kind of pride Ezekiel 29 denounces me when I imagine that I can sustain my own life without relying on God?
How does the promise that God strengthens his people calls me to expect restoration even after periods of discipline and humiliation?
study.practice: This week, examine an area where you usually seek security outside of God: finances, relationships, status, control or personal plans. Pray confessing this dependence and replace an attitude of excessive trust with a concrete practice of faith, such as asking for wisdom before deciding, seeking reconciliation or serving without seeking recognition. Also read the chapter remembering that God not only judges the pride of the nations, but strengthens his people so that his mouth may open with courage and truth.
study.uncertainty: Some historical details in the notes are presented as hypotheses or reconstructions of commentators, especially the exact identification of Pharaoh and certain geographical terms such as Patros. The reading of "doing grows" in verse 21 is interpretative in the notes, and can be understood more broadly as a renewal of Israel's strength and dignity.
